task_1.title: Remove Python 3.7 collection ABC deprecation warnings
task_1.description: This patch updates abstract collection compatibility handling so the library no longer emits Python 3.7 deprecation warnings while preserving existing mapping and mutable-container behavior at runtime.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading from 2.10.1 to 2.10.2 removes Python 3.7 deprecation warnings related to abstract collection types without changing how mapping-like and mutable container objects are recognized by the library.

expectation.grounded: The library should resolve abstract collection base classes through its compatibility layer using `collections.abc` when available, while preserving the observable contracts that `Context` is recognized as a `Mapping`, `LRUCache` is recognized as a `MutableMapping`, `_MagicFormatMapping` behaves as a `Mapping`, the built-in `mapping` test checks against `abc.Mapping`, and sandbox mutability checks continue to rely on `abc.MutableSet`, `abc.MutableMapping`, and `abc.MutableSequence`.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should eliminate deprecation noise on newer Python runtimes while keeping template behavior, mapping detection, and sandbox container classification consistent with previous releases.

constraints.grounded: Compatibility must be preserved across supported Python versions by falling back when `collections.abc` is not exposed separately. The change must not alter the outcome of mapping or mutable-container classification beyond removing warnings tied to deprecated imports.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must be backward-compatible and should not introduce behavior changes other than stopping the deprecated collection ABC usage from surfacing warnings.

behavior: Importing and using the library on Python versions that deprecate `collections.Mapping` and related aliases should no longer emit deprecation warnings for those abstract collection types.
The built-in `mapping` test should continue to return true for values recognized by the standard mapping abstract base class.
Runtime `Context` objects should remain recognized as mapping instances through abstract base class registration.
`LRUCache` objects should remain recognized as mutable mapping instances through abstract base class registration.
Sandbox mutability checks should continue to classify mutable sets, mappings, and sequences using the corresponding abstract base class semantics.
acceptance_criteria: When the library is imported or exercised on Python 3.7 or newer, it should not emit deprecation warnings caused by importing abstract collection types from `collections`.
When a value implements the standard mapping abstract base class, the built-in `mapping` test should continue to identify it as a mapping.
When runtime features interact with `Context`, it should still satisfy mapping-type checks expected by existing integrations.
When runtime features interact with `LRUCache`, it should still satisfy mutable-mapping checks expected by existing integrations.
When sandbox logic evaluates mutable container types, it should preserve the same set, mapping, and sequence classification behavior as before the upgrade.

task_2.title: Prevent sandboxed range memory exhaustion on Python 2
task_2.description: Sandboxed template range evaluation now preserves the sandbox size guard on Python 2 so very large ranges are rejected safely instead of attempting to allocate the full sequence in memory. This restores predictable OverflowError behavior for blocked inputs while keeping normal sandboxed range iteration available for allowed sizes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that using `range(...)` inside a sandboxed template enforces the sandbox range-size limit safely on Python 2, so oversized ranges raise `OverflowError` instead of exhausting memory.

expectation.grounded: In `SandboxedEnvironment`, the exposed sandboxed `range` helper backed by `jinja2.sandbox.safe_range` must continue enforcing `MAX_RANGE` by computed range length. On Python 2, evaluating very large ranges must not require materializing the full sequence before the limit check; if the resulting range length exceeds `MAX_RANGE`, `safe_range` should raise `OverflowError`, and otherwise return a normal iterable range result.
expectation.conceptual: Sandboxed templates should support normal `range(...)` usage for allowed sizes, while oversized ranges are rejected predictably with `OverflowError` rather than causing excessive memory use.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the observable sandbox contract for valid ranges: calls whose computed length is at or below `MAX_RANGE` must remain iterable with normal `range(start, stop, step)` semantics, and the overflow guard must still be based on the length of the produced range, not just the raw numeric magnitude of an argument.
constraints.conceptual: Keep ordinary sandboxed range iteration working as before, and only block ranges that exceed the documented sandbox size limit.

behavior: When sandboxed `range(...)` is evaluated on Python 2, the size check is performed without constructing the full sequence in memory.
If the computed range length is greater than `MAX_RANGE`, sandboxed evaluation raises `OverflowError` before iteration proceeds.
If the computed range length is `MAX_RANGE` or smaller, the sandboxed range remains usable for normal template iteration.
The range-size protection applies to large numeric inputs that would otherwise create extremely large sequences during sandboxed rendering.
acceptance_criteria: When a sandboxed template evaluates `range(total)` and the resulting range length is greater than the sandbox maximum, rendering should fail with `OverflowError`.
When a sandboxed template evaluates `range(total)` and the resulting range length is equal to or below the sandbox maximum, rendering should proceed and iterate over the expected values.
When running under Python 2, requesting an extremely large sandboxed range should be rejected by the sandbox limit instead of attempting to allocate the entire sequence in memory.

task_3.title: Avoid debug-build crashes during traceback rewriting
task_3.description: Jinja2 2.10.2 updates its traceback rewriting behavior for Python 3.7 and newer to use native traceback support instead of the older low-level fallback, preventing interpreter crashes on debug builds while preserving error-reporting behavior across supported Python versions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Jinja2 can rewrite template-related tracebacks on Python 3.7 and newer without crashing the interpreter, including on CPython debug builds, while preserving compatible traceback behavior on older supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: When Jinja2 debug traceback processing needs to relink traceback objects, Python 3.7 and newer should use direct traceback `tb_next` assignment rather than the legacy low-level fallback. This should prevent interpreter aborts or core dumps seen on debug builds and still allow Jinja2 to present rewritten template tracebacks. On Python 3.6 and older, the existing fallback path remains available as a best-effort compatibility mechanism.
expectation.conceptual: Template and undefined-related failures should continue to produce usable Jinja2-managed tracebacks, but modern Python runtimes must no longer be destabilized by the traceback-rewriting step.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress Jinja2's ability to chain and expose rewritten tracebacks for template errors. Preserve compatibility behavior for Python 3.6 and older, where native traceback relinking support is not available, and keep older-runtime fallback initialization non-fatal if it cannot be enabled.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must preserve existing error-reporting behavior and backward compatibility for older supported runtimes, and it must not replace the original crash with a new initialization or runtime failure.

behavior: On Python 3.7 and newer, Jinja2 relinks traceback chains through the native traceback object interface instead of low-level memory manipulation.
On CPython debug builds, operations that trigger Jinja2 traceback rewriting should no longer abort the interpreter or produce a core dump.
Rewritten Jinja2 tracebacks should remain available to callers after the change, rather than disabling traceback chaining on Python 3.7 and newer.
On Python 3.6 and older, Jinja2 continues to use the prior best-effort fallback behavior for traceback relinking.
acceptance_criteria: When Jinja2 processes a template-related exception on Python 3.7 or newer, it should be able to relink the traceback chain without crashing the Python process.
When the same behavior occurs on a CPython debug build, execution should complete normally rather than aborting or dumping core.
When Jinja2 rewrites a traceback on Python 3.7 or newer, the resulting exception should still expose linked traceback information through normal Python exception handling.
When the library runs on Python 3.6 or older, existing traceback-handling behavior should continue without introducing a new hard failure during setup or error processing.
